strengths: Careful, well-motivated component identification study (Table 1) that empirically justifies placing the task-synergy memory at the post-MHSA projection layer, rather than assuming a design choice.

The proposed HEE sampling strategy, which leverages task-specific CLS token similarity to bias the SPOS supernet training and evolutionary search, is a sensible and reasonably novel idea, and the paper provides convincing ablations (Table 4, Fig. 7) showing it substantially outperforms vanilla uniform (PE) sampling both in accuracy and parameter efficiency.

Extensive experimental validation across two benchmarks (VDD, 5-Dataset), two protocols (sequential/continual and task-to-task transfer), multiple random seeds, and five different task orderings, with consistent qualitative trends in the learned architecture (Figs. 4, 10, 14-17).

Efficiency analysis is included, showing CHEEM adds far fewer FLOPs per task than prompt-based methods due to avoiding growth in the quadratic-cost MHSA token length, which is a meaningful practical advantage.

Thorough appendix with reproducibility details (hyperparameters, data splits, augmentation choices, baseline modification details) and an honest ablation on an implementation choice (shortcut in Adapt) that could have been cherry-picked but instead reports the less favorable option is used in the main results.

Reasonable and mostly-fair re-implementation and adaptation of several prior baselines (L2P, S-Prompts, SupSup, EFT, LL, L2G with DARTS/β-DARTS) to work with ViTs and the task-incremental VDD setting, which is a nontrivial engineering contribution that benefits the community for future comparisons.
weaknesses: The method fundamentally requires task ID at inference (task-incremental setting only); the paper acknowledges this as a limitation but offers no solution, which limits the real-world applicability relative to class/domain-incremental methods that are increasingly the focus of the field.

The absolute performance gains are modest given the added complexity: ~3.3% average accuracy improvement on VDD and only ~1% on 5-Dataset over the best baseline, while the proposed pipeline (supernet training + evolutionary search + retraining/finetuning per task) is considerably more expensive and complex than simple prompt-based or single-pass adapter methods; no wall-clock training time comparison is provided to contextualize this trade-off.

The paper notes an unresolved discrepancy between the sequential-continual and task-to-task transfer variants of CHEEM (Section 3.1.2), where the same NAS approach produces qualitatively different behavior and the authors admit 'there is some room for improvement,' indicating the HEE-NAS formulation is not fully robust/consistent across settings.

Comparisons to prompt-based baselines (L2P, S-Prompts) may be somewhat unbalanced since those methods use a frozen backbone by design and were adapted post hoc to use task ID for prompt retrieval, whereas CHEEM directly grows/updates the backbone; a more recent/stronger prompt-based baseline (e.g., CODA-Prompt, DualPrompt) mentioned in related work is not empirically compared despite being available.

Only a single backbone variant (ViT-B/8, custom low-resolution training) is evaluated; no results with larger-scale pretrained backbones (e.g., ViT-B/16, CLIP) are shown despite the introduction motivating the work with such models, limiting generality claims.

Scalability to longer task sequences beyond 10 tasks is untested, and the per-layer combinatorial search space (which grows with the number of prior tasks/experts) raises scalability concerns for long streams that are not discussed quantitatively (e.g., growth in supernet size or search cost over many tasks).

The comparison in Table 3 against EWC/L2-regularization/Experience Replay uses only 20 training epochs versus 100+30 for CHEEM, which, while plausibly justified by faster convergence of those methods, is not rigorously controlled and could be seen as an unequal comparison undermining the forgetting analysis.

strengths: Addresses a practically important but underexplored setting: ExfCCL on realistic, class/data-imbalanced benchmarks (MTIL, VDD) with both large (ViT-Base) and tiny (DEiT-Tiny) backbones, rather than only balanced Split-ImageNet-R style setups.

The core technical idea—decomposing backbone adaptation into four interpretable primitives (Reuse, New, Adapt, Skip) combined with a hierarchical exploration-exploitation sampling scheme for supernet training and evolutionary search—is a reasonably novel extension of prior learning-to-grow/SPOS style NAS to ViTs and continual learning, with a principled task-similarity-driven sampling mechanism rather than naive uniform sampling.

Extensive empirical evaluation: two backbones, two benchmarks, many baselines (prompting-based, PEFT-based, regularization-based, and two recent adapter methods), several ablations (CHEEM placement, HEE vs. uniform sampling, exploration probability, tolerance threshold, task order robustness, lightweight task-ID backbones, CLIP backbone generalization).

Qualitative results (Figs. 3, 6-9) showing that the learned architectures are semantically sensible (e.g., skipping blocks for easy tasks like MNIST/EuroSAT, adding new/adapt operations for tasks with larger distribution shift) provide good supporting evidence beyond aggregate metrics.

Inclusion of a theoretical analysis (Appendix I) of the local vs. global argmax discrepancy for task-agnostic heads is a nice addition that helps explain why prompting-based baselines underperform in this setting.
Reasonably transparent reporting of overhead (Table 7, FLOPs including task-ID inference cost) rather than hiding these costs, and reporting variance across seeds for most results.
weaknesses: The method still requires explicit task-ID inference at test time via an external task-centroid memory borrowed from prior work (S-Prompts), which is a substantial dependency not core to the paper's contribution yet materially affects reported accuracy and roughly doubles FLOPs; the paper does not deeply analyze robustness/sensitivity of the whole pipeline to task-ID misclassification.

The proposed Figure-of-Merit metric multiplicatively combines an accuracy-gap ratio and a FLOPs ratio, which can produce extreme, hard-to-interpret values (e.g., FoM values in the thousands in Table 1) especially when the accuracy gap to the upper bound approaches zero; the paper acknowledges this effect but does not fully address whether such large FoM numbers are meaningful for practical comparison.

Missing comparisons against some more recent, closely related continual-learning/backbone-adaptation methods that are cited (e.g., InfLoRA, SD-LoRA) but not benchmarked, leaving open whether CHEEM's gains hold against the strongest recent competitors.

Limited analysis of scalability: as the number of streaming tasks T grows, the supernet search space (experts per layer) grows with T, but there is no discussion or empirical study of NAS search cost/memory as a function of number of tasks beyond the datasets tested (11-12 tasks).

The ablation comparing HEE vs. uniform sampling (Table 9) shows comparable accuracy with HEE mainly reducing parameter growth; some of the headline accuracy improvements over the LoRA-CL special case are modest (e.g., ~1% for ViT-Base) and reported only across three seeds, raising questions about the statistical significance of some comparisons.
Reported task-wise FLOPs savings for easier tasks (Table 6) are relatively modest in absolute terms, somewhat tempering the claimed benefit of task-difficulty-aware compute allocation.
The code repository link is a placeholder/broken (https://github.com/), limiting reproducibility verification at review time.

The paper lacks an explicit limitations section discussing failure modes (e.g., when task-ID inference is wrong, or when tasks are highly ambiguous/overlapping) despite the method's reliance on accurate task identification.

strengths: Identifies an underexplored design space in ExfCCL backbone adaptation by introducing New and Skip operations alongside the more common Reuse/Adapt, and cleanly motivates why prompting-based and pure parameter-tuning methods each fail to be task-difficulty/synergy aware.

Extensive empirical evaluation on two genuinely challenging, class/data-imbalanced benchmarks (MTIL, VDD) with two backbone scales (ViT-Base, DEiT-Tiny) and an additional CLIP backbone in the supplementary, which is broader than most ExfCCL papers that only test balanced benchmarks with large backbones.

Thorough set of ablations: CHEEM placement (MLP-down vs projection), HEE vs. uniform sampling, exploration probability schedule, evolutionary search tolerance threshold, task order sensitivity, and a lightweight external-memory variant (CHEEMlite) — these substantially strengthen the empirical case.

Qualitative results (Figs. 3, 6-9) showing the learned architectures are sensible and correlate with intuitive task difficulty/similarity (e.g., more Skip on MNIST/EuroSAT, more New/Adapt on fine-grained or highly dissimilar tasks) provide interpretability rarely seen in NAS-based continual learning work.

A useful theoretical/empirical dissection (Appendix I) of the local-vs-global argmax discrepancy that explains why prompting methods with task-agnostic heads underperform, adding scientific insight beyond just reporting numbers.

CHEEM consistently and substantially outperforms strong prompting baselines and closely approaches full fine-tuning/LoRA fine-tuning upper bounds while using less compute than several baselines, which is a meaningful practical contribution, especially for the underexplored tiny-backbone setting.
weaknesses: The proposed Figure-of-Merit metric is a multiplicative ratio of accuracy-gap-to-upper-bound and FLOPs that can produce extreme, hard-to-interpret values (e.g., FoM=4538.8) whenever a baseline's accuracy gap to the upper bound approaches zero in the denominator; the metric's sensitivity to this near-singularity is not discussed, and its absolute magnitudes convey little intuitive meaning beyond rank ordering.

CHEEM requires task-ID inference via an extra forward pass through the backbone (external memory), which the paper acknowledges roughly doubles inference FLOPs relative to the reported upper bounds; the main comparison tables mix this hidden cost inconsistently with baselines, making some FLOPs comparisons less apples-to-apples than presented.

The core technical machinery (SPOS-style supernet training, evolutionary NAS from Real et al., LoRA adaptation, and an external task-centroid memory adapted directly from S-Prompts) is largely assembled from existing components; the primary novel contribution is the hierarchical similarity-based sampling scheme and the Reuse/New/Adapt/Skip search space itself, which is a comparatively incremental extension of L2G to ViTs.

The HEE vs. uniform sampling ablation (Table 9) shows nearly identical average accuracy (e.g., 84.74 vs 85.88 on ViT-Base, 75.05 vs 74.51 on DEiT-Tiny), with the main benefit of HEE being parameter parsimony rather than accuracy; this somewhat undercuts the claimed importance of the hierarchical exploration-exploitation sampling for performance per se.

Scalability of the internal memory is not analyzed: since New operations add full layers per task, it is unclear how parameter count and search cost grow as the number of streaming tasks increases well beyond the 11-12 tasks tested, which is an important practical concern for a memory-based continual learning method.

Reproducibility is currently unverifiable since the code repository link is a placeholder without a working URL, and important supernet/evolutionary-search hyperparameters (population size, number of generations, mutation details) are only partially specified.

Results are reported over only three seeds without formal significance testing, and some comparative claims (e.g., CHEEM vs LoRA-CL gains on ViT-Base being only ~1%) suggest the benefit of the full NAS pipeline over the simpler LoRA-only ablation is modest for stronger backbones, raising a question about when the added complexity is truly necessary versus the simpler LoRA-CL baseline.
